variants.title: Run the world-model loop
variants.context: A world model drives a loop: observe a partial view, infer a latent state, imagine action outcomes, choose a bounded plan while penalizing uncertainty, then execute one action and return to reality before extending anything further.
variants.prompt: A warehouse robot must round a shelf it cannot see behind. Put the loop steps in order.

items.text: Choose a bounded plan: rank the trajectories, penalize uncertainty, and reject plans that cross a safety boundary.
Observe a partial view: take the current camera frame and telemetry as evidence, not as full state.
Act once and correct: execute a limited action, observe reality again, and shorten the plan when evidence disagrees.
Imagine action outcomes: advance the learned dynamics under candidate actions and predict reward and constraints.
Infer a latent state: combine the observation with prior state and the previous action to estimate hidden variables.

variants.hint: How much of the imagined plan is the agent allowed to execute before it looks again?
variants.explanation: Receding-horizon control executes only the first action and replans, which repeatedly anchors imagination to fresh evidence.

variants.title: Run the world-model loop
variants.context: A world model drives a loop: observe a partial view, infer a latent state, imagine action outcomes, choose a bounded plan while penalizing uncertainty, then execute one action and return to reality before extending anything further.
variants.prompt: A sensor drops out for two frames and the agent must keep moving safely. Put the loop steps in order.

items.text: Choose a bounded plan: prefer the plan whose worst explanation still respects the hard constraint.
Observe a partial view: register that the expected measurement is missing rather than treating it as empty.
Infer a latent state: carry forward evidence that is no longer visible and keep several explanations alive.
Imagine action outcomes: roll out candidate actions from the widened belief instead of one guessed state.
Act once and correct: take the conservative action and update the belief as soon as the sensor returns.

variants.hint: What does a belief state hold that the latest frame does not?
variants.explanation: A belief state remembers evidence that has left the frame and keeps uncertainty separate from a single guessed state.

variants.title: Run the world-model loop
variants.context: A world model drives a loop: observe a partial view, infer a latent state, imagine action outcomes, choose a bounded plan while penalizing uncertainty, then execute one action and return to reality before extending anything further.
variants.prompt: Halfway through a plan, the observed next state disagrees with the imagined one. Put the loop steps in order for the following cycle.

items.text: Infer a latent state: correct the belief from the new evidence rather than continuing from the predicted state.
Imagine action outcomes: re-roll the candidate actions from the corrected state over a shortened horizon.
Observe a partial view: read the real next observation that contradicts the imagined transition.
Act once and correct: execute one action and check again before extending the horizon.
Choose a bounded plan: discard the remainder of the stale plan and rank freshly imagined trajectories.

variants.hint: A plan built from a state that turned out wrong has no remaining claim.
variants.explanation: Real observations replace imagined state on a defined cadence, and a contradicted plan is shortened or abandoned rather than continued.

variants.title: Respond to divergence
variants.context: When imagination and reality disagree the response is ordered: contain the stale rollout, fall back to a controller with an explicit envelope, preserve the divergence trace, then repair evidence and boundaries before release.
variants.prompt: Ensemble disagreement rises sharply and the proposed plan crosses a hard risk limit. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Fall back: hand control to a conservative policy or stop whose operating envelope is explicit.
Contain: reject the current plan because the uncertainty budget and the hard constraint were both crossed.
Recover: add representative real data, recalibrate uncertainty, and narrow the horizon before release.
Diagnose: preserve observations, actions, latent states, ensemble predictions, and planner scores.

variants.hint: The first move is to stop extending the rollout, not to explain it.
variants.explanation: A crossed safety boundary ends the plan immediately, and analysis happens after control is back inside a known envelope.

variants.title: Respond to divergence
variants.context: When imagination and reality disagree the response is ordered: contain the stale rollout, fall back to a controller with an explicit envelope, preserve the divergence trace, then repair evidence and boundaries before release.
variants.prompt: Observed residuals against the imagined trajectory climb in one weather regime only. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Recover: collect representative data for that regime and shorten the credible horizon there.
Fall back: run the rule-based controller whose envelope covers this regime.
Contain: stop extending rollouts in that regime once residuals cross their boundary.
Diagnose: store the divergence traces for the regime alongside the planner's scores and outcomes.

variants.hint: The horizon that is credible in one regime is not automatically credible in another.
variants.explanation: The credible planning horizon is tracked by regime and shortened automatically when residuals or disagreement rise.

variants.title: Respond to divergence
variants.context: When imagination and reality disagree the response is ordered: contain the stale rollout, fall back to a controller with an explicit envelope, preserve the divergence trace, then repair evidence and boundaries before release.
variants.prompt: A reward head was mislabeled, so imagined return looks high on trajectories the operator would refuse. Put the response steps in order.

items.text: Diagnose: keep the traces linking planner scores, safety decisions, and actual outcomes.
Fall back: return to the previous controller while the objective is in doubt.
Recover: fix the objective, recalibrate uncertainty, and re-narrow the operating domain before release.
Contain: reject the plans whose predicted return depends on the suspect head.

variants.hint: An objective error is repaired in the model, not compensated for in the planner.
variants.explanation: Recovery repairs evidence, objectives, sensors, and boundaries, and release waits until the repaired model has been re-evaluated.

variants.title: Pick the evidence that settles it
variants.context: Prediction quality is measured where planning uses it. A one-step holdout, an open-loop rollout holdout, a policy-conditioned holdout, and a real control trial each answer a different question and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: A team plans its world-model evaluation. Match each set to what it detects.

pairs.label: One-step holdout
pairs.detail: Local transition, reward, continuation, and observation-prediction errors near the data.

pairs.label: Open-loop rollout holdout
pairs.detail: Error accumulation when predicted state is fed back without correction.

pairs.label: Policy-conditioned holdout
pairs.detail: States the current planner visits, including actions the collection policy rarely chose.

pairs.label: Real control trial
pairs.detail: Task return, safety constraints, recovery, and action ranking under a bounded deployment protocol.

variants.hint: Ask which set contains the states the planner will actually reach.
variants.explanation: The four sets answer different questions, so a strong score on one of them says nothing about the others.

variants.title: Pick the evidence that settles it
variants.context: Prediction quality is measured where planning uses it. A one-step holdout, an open-loop rollout holdout, a policy-conditioned holdout, and a real control trial each answer a different question and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: Four questions come up in review. Match each question to the set that answers it.

pairs.label: Does error compound once the model consumes its own predictions?
pairs.detail: The open-loop rollout holdout, which feeds predictions back.

pairs.label: Is the next-step reward head accurate near the training data?
pairs.detail: The one-step holdout, which isolates local prediction error.

pairs.label: Does the model cover the states this new planner now visits?
pairs.detail: The policy-conditioned holdout, gathered under the current planner.

pairs.label: Does the system recover safely when a constraint is approached?
pairs.detail: The real control trial, run under a bounded deployment protocol.

variants.hint: Two of these questions differ only in whether predictions are fed back.
variants.explanation: Evaluation sets stay separate so that a change of planner or horizon does not quietly invalidate the evidence behind a release.

variants.title: Pick the evidence that settles it
variants.context: Prediction quality is measured where planning uses it. A one-step holdout, an open-loop rollout holdout, a policy-conditioned holdout, and a real control trial each answer a different question and none of them substitutes for another.
variants.prompt: The team reports four numbers about planning quality. Match each report to what it establishes.

pairs.label: Error and calibration at every planning depth from one to the horizon
pairs.detail: Whether the model still holds up at the depth the planner uses.

pairs.label: Results sliced by contact, speed, weather, object, and map
pairs.detail: Whether coverage holds across control-relevant regimes.

pairs.label: Whether model and reality prefer the same candidate action
pairs.detail: Decision agreement, which is what a planner actually consumes.

pairs.label: Constraint prediction, uncertainty coverage, and recovery behavior
pairs.detail: Whether the safety boundary is measured rather than assumed.

variants.hint: Which of these is closest to the quantity the planner consumes?
variants.explanation: Decision usefulness, not visual realism, is the invariant, so evidence is reported at planning depth and in terms of action ranking.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: World models fail in named ways: observation aliasing, missing action effects, compounding rollout error, model exploitation, uncalibrated confidence, objective mismatch, and unsafe transfer. Naming the failure decides the fix.
variants.prompt: A robot behind a shelf is invisible in the latest frame, and two very different hidden situations produce nearly identical images. The agent picks an unsafe action. Which failure is this?
options: Observation aliasing, since different hidden states produce measurements the latest frame cannot separate.
Compounding error, since small transition errors push a long rollout into unsupported latent regions.
Model exploitation, since the planner has found imagined high-reward states caused by model error.
optionFeedback: Correct: occlusion and noise let distinct states look alike, which is why control needs a belief state rather than a frame.
Compounding error grows with rollout depth, but here the very first inference is already ambiguous.
Exploitation shows up as high imagined return on odd trajectories, not as two situations that look the same.
variants.hint: Ask whether the problem appeared before any imagining started.
variants.explanation: Aliasing is an inference failure, so the fix is a latent belief that retains prior evidence rather than a longer or better rollout.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: World models fail in named ways: observation aliasing, missing action effects, compounding rollout error, model exploitation, uncalibrated confidence, objective mismatch, and unsafe transfer. Naming the failure decides the fix.
variants.prompt: Imagined return climbs every iteration while real return falls, and the winning plans all route through rare action sequences the data barely contains. Which failure is this?
options: Uncalibrated confidence, since low ensemble disagreement was mistaken for correctness off support.
Model exploitation, since the policy is optimizing errors in the learned model instead of the task.
Missing action effects, since the model predicts what usually happens rather than the counterfactual.
optionFeedback: Miscalibration is often the enabler here, but the described symptom is the policy profiting from model error.
Correct: rising imagined return with falling real return along rare action paths is the signature of exploitation.
Missing action effects would flatten the difference between actions, not concentrate return on rare sequences.
variants.hint: Follow which quantity is going up and which is going down.
variants.explanation: Exploitation is detected by searching for high predicted return paired with unusual state or action sequences, not by better reconstructions.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: World models fail in named ways: observation aliasing, missing action effects, compounding rollout error, model exploitation, uncalibrated confidence, objective mismatch, and unsafe transfer. Naming the failure decides the fix.
variants.prompt: Reconstruction loss improves every week, yet the model and reality increasingly disagree about which candidate action is best. Which failure is this?
options: Unsafe transfer, since simulated success was promoted without controlled evidence in the same regime.
Objective mismatch, since visual prediction improved while reward and action ranking got worse.
Compounding error, since predicted state is fed back and drifts away from the training distribution.
optionFeedback: Unsafe transfer describes how a model was released, not why sharper images track worse decisions.
Correct: a sharp next-frame model can miss contact, reward, or hazard dynamics that decide the action.
Compounding error would show up as depth-dependent degradation rather than a steady divergence in ranking.
variants.hint: Compare what the loss rewards with what the planner consumes.
variants.explanation: The invariant is decision usefulness, so a model is judged by whether imagined action consequences still rank actions the way reality does.

variants.title: Decide what the model must predict
variants.context: Before training, decide what the model must predict: the representation target, the dynamics target, the control target, the task heads, and the correction cadence. The right objective preserves the distinctions that change action ranking.
variants.prompt: A search-based controller acts in an environment whose observations are expensive to reconstruct and largely irrelevant to the outcome. Which representation target fits?
options: Predict learned features of the next observation so reconstruction cost drops but detail is kept.
Preserve only reward, policy, and value-relevant information so search stays effective.
Reconstruct future observations so the learned state can be inspected frame by frame.
optionFeedback: Feature prediction is cheaper than pixels, but it still optimizes for describing observations rather than ranking actions.
Correct: a value-equivalent model learns transitions plus reward, policy, and value predictions that make search work.
Reconstruction spends capacity on detail that never changes which action the search prefers.
variants.hint: What has to be true for the search to rank actions correctly?
variants.explanation: The representation target should preserve exactly the distinctions that change action ranking in the intended operating regime.

variants.title: Decide what the model must predict
variants.context: Before training, decide what the model must predict: the representation target, the dynamics target, the control target, the task heads, and the correction cadence. The right objective preserves the distinctions that change action ranking.
variants.prompt: A planner needs to know when to stop trusting its own rollout. Which dynamics target supports that gate?
options: Predict a single next latent state and treat the residual against reality as the trust signal.
Predict an ensemble whose disagreement estimates epistemic uncertainty at each rollout step.
Predict a distribution over the next observation and use its variance as the trust signal.
optionFeedback: A single point prediction gives no measure of what the model does not know until reality arrives.
Correct: ensemble disagreement gives a per-step epistemic signal the planner can penalize and gate on.
Observation variance describes sensing noise more than it describes the model being outside its support.
variants.hint: Which signal is available before the action is taken?
variants.explanation: Uncertainty that is not calibrated cannot define a trustworthy gate, so the dynamics target must produce a usable uncertainty estimate.

variants.title: Decide what the model must predict
variants.context: Before training, decide what the model must predict: the representation target, the dynamics target, the control target, the task heads, and the correction cadence. The right objective preserves the distinctions that change action ranking.
variants.prompt: Real interaction on a physical arm is slow and risky, and the team wants many policy updates per real episode. Which control target fits?
options: Train actor and critic on trajectories imagined in the learned latent model between real episodes.
Run online trajectory search at every control step and skip learning a policy altogether.
Collect more real episodes first so the policy can be updated from environment interaction only.
optionFeedback: Correct: learning the actor and critic in imagination is what removes the need for a real step per policy update.
Online search still helps at control time, but it does not give the policy the extra updates the team asked for.
More real interaction is exactly the expensive resource the world model exists to conserve.
variants.hint: Count how many real environment steps each option costs per policy update.
variants.explanation: The control target says where improvement comes from, and imagined trajectories are what buy policy updates without extra real interaction.
